title: Sersa Victory: Choice Design in Roguelikes
speaker: Sersa Victory
description:
Meaningful player choice is essential to games of all genres, and this short talk provides an overview of the major choice types that appear in games: mutually exclusive actions, risk versus reward, now versus later, resource trade, and dilemma.

To help illustrate each choice type, this talk highlights examples from popular games in the genre such as NetHack, Brogue, Forays into Norrendrin, Dungeon Crawl Stone Soup, and the original Rogue. This talk also touches on choice-driven elements I added to my own reimagining of Rogue and suggests ideas for choices developers might experiment with in their projects.

Ultimately, this talk aims to give developers a vocabulary for designing choices that can help make their roguelikes more challenging, dramatic, and engaging.

Lead-in music generated by Sonat Uzun.

I want to get into the meat of the talk. The types of engaging choices in games.
In this section, I will describe five different types of engaging choices
mutually exclusive actions, risk versus reward, now versus later, resource trade and dilemma.
I will illustrate each choice type by drawing on examples from popular traditional roguelikes.
The first choice type I would like to describe is mutually exclusive action. In a mutually exclusive
action choice the player has multiple things she would like to do but she want do them all.
This is in essence the basic tradeoff. The player must weigh the benefits of one course
of action over the opportunity cost of north naught not picking the other courses of action.
A great illustration is your turn in any traditional roguelike.
Typically the player only gets one action on her turn before the monster
and environment take their turn. There might be several things she would like to do,
drink a potion, swap her magical rings and zap the charging troll with fireballs,
however she will only be able to choose one of these actions and in crunch moments where every
turn counts, and one wrong move could mean permadeath, this choice can be quite tense.
Another great example of a mutually exclusive choice are the treasure rooms in my favorite
roguelike Brogue. These rooms contain several treasures each with their own unique benefits.
Once the player takes the item off the pedestal cages drop down and she can only choose one item
it leave with. There is not necessarily a write or wrong answer here. The player must assess
which option to choose based on her play style, her build,
what's happened so far in the game, and what she predicts might come later.
The final example I am give of a mutually exclusive choice are the skill shrines in Forays
into Norrendrin. These shirines come in pairs and if she accepts the benefit of one the other goes
inert thus the player must think carefully about which skill she prefer to level up.
People think about choices in games they often think abet about this one -- risk versus reward.
The player has an option between a lower risk, lower reward and a higher risk/higher reward
option. Such choices challenge the player to assess the value of a potential award
relative to her ability to mitigate the risks of seeking that reward. Maybe one of the most iconic
risk versus reward choices in traditional roguelike is the use of unidentified items.
The player must weigh the peril of using an unknown item that might be dangerous or cursed
against the direness of her situation. If the player is surrounded by monsters, is using an
unknown scroll and hoping it is teleport worth the risk of it being explosive ruins instead?
Another common element of traditional roguelikes that present a risk-reward choice are out of depth
monsters. These enemies appear on dungeon levels much earlier than they would normally thus posing
a serious threat however defeating such monsters could earn significant experience points and loot.
The player must weigh whether she feels confident or equipped enough to engage with an out of depth
monster or if it is better to steer clear. A third element are vaults. Chambers teaming with
dangerous monsters and powerful treasures. When encountering a vault, the player must
choose whether the treasures present justify the risk of engaging with a horde of tough enemies.
The next type of choice I would like to describe is the now versus later choice. The player has a
limited resource in these situations. If she uses it now she can't use it later.
The player alternatively can have something modest or holdout for something better. Now versus later
choices challenge the player to balance short term immediate needs versus or long term goals.
Consumable items or items with a limited number of uses are a common example of a now versus
later choice in traditional roguelikes. Items such as potions or scrolls can only be used
once and then they are gone. Likewise wands can only be zapped so many times before they fills.
In any given situation, the player must assess whether it warrents using that item up or if it
is smarter to hold on to it for potentially more serious situation later. Forays into Norrendrin
includes what might be my favorite example of a now versus later choice in traditional roguelikes.
Unlike many other roguelikes which allow recovery when you find a corner, foray gives one action
recovery per dungeon level and this creates an interesting tension as the player must decide
how serious her situation truly is before using up her one opportunity to rest per dungeon level. The
third example of a now versus later comes from my own remake of roguelike and the player can
become a priestess to one of three Godesses by praying at a higher alter. She encounters early
in the game where she can become a les important priestess but if she does she want pray at the one
to become a high priestess. The player must assess how early she needs it in her run or
if she feels confident enough she can survive to the deeper levels and earn being a high priestess.
The fourth choice type I would like to talk about is resource trade.
In a resource trade the player can trade something she has for something she doesn't.
The thing being traded for is typically useful in a different way
or in a different context than the thing that she is trading away. An example resource trade
in traditional roguelikes are the Black Smith forages in ADOM. These can be used to repair or
enhance weapons and armor but doing so requires the player to spend metal ingots. The player can
meltdown other metallic items in the inventory thus trading them for attack or defense buft.
The magic lamp in NetHack doesn't run out of oil thus making it extremely useful in navigating
the dark and perilous levels and the player can choose to rub the lamp to summon a genie
and make a wish but it turns the magic lamp into an ordinary oil lamp that will burnout
thus the player must decide if and when she wants to trade one resource for a different resource. A
third and final example of a resource trade choice comes from my remake of Rogue.
The player can encounter inert golems with a slot in
the chest and if a player gives up the magical ring to put it in the slot
the ring is lost and the Golem comes to life and fights alongside the player. The player must weigh
the value of her magical ring power against the value of having a tough bodyguard monster.
The fifth and final choice is dilemma. In a dilemma the player has failed in some way
and is forced to choose between two or more things to give up or punishment.
Failing could mean stumbling into a track, falling victim to a powerful monsterability,
using a cursed item, solving a puzzle incorrectbly and so on.

In the last few minutes of my talk I will suggest high-level ideas for
choices you might experiment with in your own traditional roguelike.
What you might do is offer the player a choice of upgrades or threats to unlock a predetermined

You may give her items, powers or spells that provide a more beneficial effect,

Before I wrap up, I want to give one final note and that is playtesting is
crucial. Sometimes a choice that looks good on paper and that embodies one of the types
described in this presentation can still end up falling flat. It is always important to get
your game in front of players and refine your choice design in response to their feedback.
Now I ran into this myself with my own remake of Rogue so here in the screenshot you will see that
the players can sometimes encounter the petrified remains of out of depth monster and smash

Choice design is a huge topic in games. This talk really only scratched the surface. However,
I hope that you found some of the concepts helpful and inspiring as you think about the
design of your own roguelikes. To very quickly summarize what I have covered, choosing is fun
and dramatic because it challenges the player to weigh tradeoffs, gives them a sense of agency,
creates moments of uncertainty and helps make the player feel smart.
Types of engaging choices you should strive for include mutually uxclusive actions,
risk versus reward, now versus later, resource trade, and dilemma. I invite you to consider
the kinds of choices your elements of the roguelike present the player and tune your
generation algorithm to layer multiple choices in an encounter. And, of course, playtesting is key.
